short: An option to sell: the right to sell the asset at the strike.
full: A put appreciates as the underlying falls, so it is bought both as a bearish bet and as portfolio insurance: losses on shares are partly offset by the put's gain. The cost of that insurance is the premium paid, and it rises the more strongly the market expects a decline. Selling a put is an obligation to buy the asset at the strike — a bet that the fall will not come.
etym: From «to put to» — the holder may put the asset to the option seller at the strike.

short: Central-bank bond buying once there is no room left to cut rates.
full: The central bank creates reserves and buys long-dated paper, lifting its price and pushing yields down at the far end of the curve. The aim is to cheapen long money when the short rate is already at zero. The side effect shows up in markets: money squeezed out of government bonds moves into equities and credit, which is why QE periods have historically coincided with rallies in risk assets.
etym: «Quantitative» because the lever is the quantity bought, not the price of money.

short: Shrinking the central bank's balance sheet: QE in reverse.
full: The central bank either sells paper or simply stops reinvesting maturing proceeds, and liquidity drains from the system. The effect is slower and duller than the policy rate but points the same way — tighter conditions. QT bites harder the thinner the market: it was the combination of balance-sheet run-off and low liquidity that produced sudden money-market rate spikes.
etym: The mirror of QE: tightening with the same lever used to ease — the size of the balance sheet.

short: The ratio of potential profit to the risk accepted on a single trade.
full: R (the risk unit) is the distance from entry to stop-loss expressed in money. 1R is the risk on a trade. A take-profit at 2R means potential profit twice the risk. Keeping a P&L journal in R lets you compare trades across instruments and account sizes. Average R over a period is the key measure of a system's quality. The "cost of indiscipline" is the difference in R between clean trades and trades that broke your rules.
etym: "R" stands for risk: one unit of risk per trade, with results measured in multiples of it.

short: A change of trend direction, from up to down or the other way round.
full: A reversal is the moment the dominant trend turns the other way. It is confirmed after the fact, by a break of structure — not by a single candle.
etym: From "to reverse" — the trend turning the other way.

short: Yield minus inflation: what is left in purchasing power.
full: A nominal 5% against 7% inflation is a real loss: more money, less to buy with it. Real yields are observed directly in inflation-linked paper — TIPS in the US. The level matters beyond the bond market: when real yields rise, assets with no cash flow — gold above all — lose appeal, because risk-free storage now has a price.
etym: In economics «real» means «adjusted for inflation», as opposed to nominal.

short: A sustained contraction in activity, not merely two weak quarters.
full: The «two quarters of falling GDP» rule is a convenient shorthand, not a definition. In the US the dating is done by the NBER, looking at employment, incomes and output together, and it announces a downturn's start with a lag of up to a year. For markets that means an awkward asymmetry: equities usually fall before the announcement and start rising well before the recession officially ends.
etym: From Latin recessio, «a retreat» — the economy retreats from the level reached.

short: A loan secured by securities with an obligation to buy them back.
full: Repo is the plumbing of the money market: a bank sells bonds agreeing to repurchase them a day later slightly dearer — borrowing against collateral. Repo rates show how ample cash is in the system, and a spike means money suddenly turned scarce. In September 2019 the US overnight rate jumped to 10% and the Fed had to inject funds on an emergency basis.
etym: Short for «repurchase agreement».

short: A broker declining to fill at the requested price and offering a new one.
full: Requotes occur with dealing-desk brokers, where the order passes through the broker's own book. Formally it is protection against filling at a stale price; in practice it is a source of complaints, because requotes arrive most often in a fast market — exactly when the entry matters most. Non-dealing models have no requotes but do have slippage: refusal is replaced by a worse price.
etym: From «to requote» — to name the price again.

short: A price level where supply has historically exceeded demand, halting a rally.
full: A resistance level is a price zone where sellers have systematically outweighed buyers. Price approaches the level, is pushed back and declines. Once broken, former resistance frequently becomes support. Traders use resistance levels to take profit and to judge how much room a move has left. Round numbers (1000, 1500, 2000) often act as psychological resistance.
etym: From "resistance" — the ceiling that slows a rally.

short: Monthly retail turnover: a direct measure of consumer demand.
full: US consumption is about two thirds of GDP, so retail sales is one of the heavier releases. It is published in nominal money, i.e. not adjusted for inflation: 3% growth with 3% inflation means the same quantity was bought. The «control group» — excluding autos, petrol and building materials — is watched separately, being steadier and feeding straight into the GDP calculation.
etym: «Retail» is sale to the final consumer, as opposed to wholesale.

short: Price returning to a broken level after moving beyond it.
full: After a break, former resistance often acts as support, and a return to it offers an entry with a closer stop — the technique's main practical merit. The price paid is missed moves: strong breakouts give no retest at all and leave without returning. Choosing between entering on the break and entering on the retest is choosing between frequency of trades and quality of entry.
etym: «Re-» as in again, «test» as in checking: the level is checked a second time, now from the other side.

short: The share of the deposit a trader knowingly accepts losing on one trade.
full: Risk is set BEFORE the entry and counted as a percentage of the deposit, not in currency: 1% of $10,000 and 1% of $1,000 are different sums but the same decision. Position size follows from risk, never the other way round: first "how much am I prepared to lose", then "how many lots that means at my stop". A common guide is 1–2% per trade: at 1%, ten losses in a row cost about 10% of the account; at 5%, half of it. Drawdown is asymmetric — recovering from −50% takes +100%. Risk not capped by a stop-loss is capped by the size of the deposit.
etym: From the Italian risco — a danger you accept knowingly.

short: The probability of losing the account entirely at a given risk per trade.
full: The measure ties three things together: risk per trade, win rate, and the losing streak the account can absorb. The arithmetic is merciless: at 10% risk per trade, a run of ten consecutive losses — and it does happen — leaves a third of the account. At 1% risk the same run takes a tenth. This is exactly why a sensible per-trade risk limit is discussed in single percentage points.
etym: A concept from game theory: the probability of total ruin for a player with finite capital.

short: Moving from an expiring future into the next maturity.
full: A futures position cannot be held past the contract's term, so it is moved: close the near contract, open the far one. The price difference produces a gain or a loss, and over long horizons this effect dominates everything else. A chart stitched from different contracts has gaps at the roll points — so historical levels on a «continuous» future must be read with care.
etym: From «to roll over» — the position is rolled into the next contract.

short: A 0–100 oscillator measuring the speed and size of price changes.
full: RSI (Relative Strength Index) is a technical indicator developed by J. Welles Wilder. Readings above 70 are traditionally called overbought, below 30 oversold. Important: overbought is not a sell signal — in a strong trend RSI can stay above 70 for a long time. RSI divergence (price rising while RSI falls) is a popular sign of a weakening trend. RSI is calculated as 100 − 100/(1 + RS), where RS is the ratio of average gains to average losses over the period.
etym: Introduced by J. Welles Wilder in 1978 in "New Concepts in Technical Trading Systems".

short: Client money is held separately from the broker's own funds.
full: The requirement exists for one case — broker insolvency: money in segregated accounts does not form part of the estate and is not used to pay the firm's debts. It is the first thing to check, and in regulated jurisdictions it is mandatory. A caveat: segregation protects against insolvency, not against trading losses or the client's own mistakes.
etym: From Latin segregare, «to separate» — funds kept apart from the firm's own assets.

short: How the contract ends: physical delivery or cash.
full: Deliverable contracts require the asset to change hands; cash-settled ones close against a settlement price. A retail trader must know which they hold: it was precisely this confusion that cost retail holders money in April 2020, when May WTI went negative — there was nowhere to store the oil and delivery was obligatory.
etym: From «to settle» — the final squaring of the parties' obligations.

short: A slice of ownership in a company: a claim on profits and a vote.
full: A shareholder is not a creditor but a part-owner: nothing is promised to them. If the company earns, they receive dividends and capital growth; if it fails, they stand last in line, behind every creditor. That asymmetry explains why equities out-earn bonds on average: the difference is payment for risk accepted, not a free gift from the market.
etym: From Latin actio in the sense of a claim, via Dutch actie — a share in a company.

short: Return above the risk-free rate divided by the volatility of results.
full: Sharpe answers «how much risk was paid for the return obtained». An important limitation: it penalises dispersion in both directions, treating a big lucky run as the same flaw as a slump. It is also nearly meaningless for strategies with rare large payouts — selling options shows a high Sharpe right up to the day it stops.
etym: After William Sharpe, the Nobel laureate who proposed the measure in 1966.

short: Selling an asset borrowed from the broker in expectation of a fall.
full: In a short sale the trader borrows an asset from the broker, sells it at the current price and undertakes to return it later. If the price falls, they buy it back cheaper, return the loan and keep the difference. If the price rises, the loss is theoretically unlimited.
etym: "Short" — being short of the asset you have sold.

short: The share of stock sold short and not yet bought back.
full: The measure is expressed as a percentage of free float, and the time to unwind is estimated in «days to cover» — how many daily volumes it would take for all shorts to repurchase. High short interest says two things at once: scepticism about the stock, and the risk of a violent upward squeeze if that scepticism proves wrong. The data are published with a lag.
etym: By analogy with open interest: the volume of short positions left open.

short: A sharp rally driven by the forced closing of short positions.
full: Shorts lose money as price rises and are called for more collateral; closing out means buying — which pushes price higher still. The process is self-sustaining until the shorts are exhausted, so moves can be absurd relative to the underlying business. Crucially, a squeeze ends just as abruptly: the fuel was coercion, not demand.
etym: From «squeeze» — the shorts are literally squeezed, with no way out.

short: A metal with a split nature: half safe haven, half industrial input.
full: Silver follows gold but with greater amplitude, because its market is smaller and the industrial component — electronics, solar panels, solder — is visible in the price. Hence the behaviour: in a haven-demand phase silver lags gold, in an expansion it leads. Traders use the gold/silver ratio as a rough gauge of which phase is in force.
etym: Code XAG: AG from argentum, silver's symbol in the periodic table.

short: The difference between the expected fill price and the actual one.
full: Slippage happens when an order fills at a worse price than requested. The causes are thin liquidity, high volatility around news, and slow order handling. Market orders are the most exposed. Limit orders remove negative slippage but may not fill at all. In scalping and HFT, slippage is a make-or-break factor.
etym: From "to slip" — the gap between the price you expected and the one you got.

short: Losing a deposit quickly and painfully, usually to excessive risk or leverage.
full: To blow up an account is to lose all the trading capital, or a large part of it, usually through absent risk management, excessive leverage or emotional trading after a run of losses.
etym: The account "blows up" — the capital is gone in one stretch.

short: An approach that reads the market through the actions of large participants — banks and hedge funds.
full: SMC (Smart Money Concepts) is a technical-analysis methodology built on the assumption that large institutional participants — banks, hedge funds, market makers — deliberately create patterns to capture liquidity before a reversal. Its key ideas are the Order Block (a zone of large orders), the Fair Value Gap, Break of Structure and Inducement. SMC is an educational framework; trade outcomes remain unpredictable.
etym: The term took hold in trading communities in the 2010s as an alternative to classical technical analysis.

short: The US benchmark overnight rate on secured repo transactions.
full: SOFR is computed from actual repo trades in Treasuries rather than a survey of banks — precisely where it differs from LIBOR, which was a survey and ended in manipulation scandals. Since 2023 SOFR has replaced LIBOR as the benchmark for loans and derivatives. Practically: floating rates reset off it, so it reaches the end borrower.
etym: Secured Overnight Financing Rate.

short: Bringing inflation down without a recession: an aim rarely achieved.
full: A soft landing means rates were raised enough to stop prices rising but not enough to break employment. The difficulty is the lag: policy reaches the economy several quarters later, so decisions must be taken on data describing the past. Historically there have been many attempts and very few indisputable successes.
etym: An aviation metaphor: the economy is landed onto falling inflation without crashing it.

short: Like Sharpe, but with only downside deviation in the denominator.
full: Sortino fixes Sharpe's chief oddity: it does not count good luck as risk. The denominator holds the dispersion of losing periods only, so a strategy with rare large gains gets a fair assessment. For asymmetric systems — trend-following, venture-like — Sortino is more informative. For symmetric ones the difference is small and the two measures agree.
etym: After Frank Sortino, who proposed the correction to Sharpe in the 1980s.

short: The index of 500 large US public companies, weighted by free float.
full: The world's principal equity benchmark: trillions of dollars of funds track it, and inclusion in the index itself creates demand for a stock. Membership is decided by a committee rather than a formula, so there is an element of selection. Concentration has risen in recent years: a handful of the largest names carry about a third of the weight, and the index is no longer quite «the market on average».
etym: Named for the Standard & Poor's agency; the index in its modern form dates from 1957.

short: The difference between the ask (buy) and bid (sell) price of an instrument.
full: The spread is the broker's implicit commission: on entry a trader is immediately down by the spread. Liquid instruments have tight spreads — EURUSD around 0.2–0.5 pips; exotic pairs and thin stocks can run to several per cent. Spreads widen around news and in low-liquidity hours — overnight, holidays. For scalping and high-frequency trading the spread is decisive.
etym: From "spread" — the gap between the buying and the selling price.

short: A token pegged to a currency, usually one-to-one with the dollar.
full: Stablecoins differ by backing: cash and government bonds, other crypto assets, or an algorithm. The third kind showed its fragility in 2022 when UST lost its peg and went to zero within days. For markets, stablecoin supply is a gauge of money ready to buy, and a deviation of their price from the dollar is a sign of stress in the system.
etym: From «stable» — a coin whose price, by design, does not change.

short: High inflation alongside stagnation — the worst combination for a central bank.
full: Normally inflation and unemployment pull in opposite directions, and the policy rate cures one at the other's expense. In stagflation both problems are present, and any decision worsens the other half: hike and you finish off growth, cut and you fuel prices. The classic episode is the 1970s, triggered by an oil shock — a rise in costs rather than demand.
etym: A blend of «stagnation» and «inflation», credited to the British politician Iain Macleod, 1965.

short: Where price sits inside the range of the last N periods, from 0 to 100.
full: The measure answers whether the close was nearer the period's high or its low. Readings above 80 and below 20 are called overbought and oversold, but in a strong trend the stochastic stays pinned in the extreme zone for a long time, and trading against it ruins accounts. It is therefore used in ranges or as confirmation, not as a standalone reversal signal.
etym: From Greek stochastikos, «able to guess» — whence «stochastic», random.

short: Splitting a share into several: price divides, ownership stake is unchanged.
full: A split creates nothing: ten shares at 100 become a hundred at 10. The point is accessibility — a small investor buys a cheaper share more easily, and liquidity improves. A reverse split does the opposite and usually signals trouble: price is lifted to stay inside the exchange's listing requirements. Historical charts must be viewed split-adjusted.
etym: From «split» — the share is divided into several smaller ones.

short: An order that activates when a price is reached and only then goes to market.
full: An important distinction: a stop-market becomes a market order once triggered and will certainly fill, though possibly far from the stated level. A stop-limit becomes a limit order and may not fill at all — which is exactly what leaves a position open in a fast decline, precisely when protection is needed. For capital protection the first type is safer.
etym: «Stop» as in the price at which a dormant order wakes and acts.

short: An order that closes a position automatically once a set loss is reached.
full: A stop-loss (SL) is a protective order that caps the loss. It sits at the level where the position is closed automatically. It is the core of risk management: without a stop, a single losing trade can wipe out an account. The 1% rule says risk no more than 1% of the deposit on one trade. Stops are placed beyond a support or resistance level, beyond a candle extreme, or by volatility (ATR × multiplier). Having stops taken out en masse is a liquidity sweep.
etym: From "stop loss" — literally, stop the loss.

short: Execution models in which the order goes out to liquidity providers.
full: STP passes the order onward with no dealer intervention. ECN matches participants' orders in a shared book, so the spread can be zero while the broker earns a commission on volume. For the client the practical difference is cost structure: on ECN a tight spread plus commission; on a standard account no commission but a wider spread. Compare the total, not one component.
etym: Straight Through Processing; Electronic Communication Network.

short: Buying a call and a put at the same strike: a bet on range, not direction.
full: A straddle wins if the market travels far either way and loses if it sits still. Breakeven is the sum of both premiums, and it is often wider than it looks: ahead of a big event IV is high, so call and put are both expensive. It happens often that the news lands, price jerks, and the straddle still loses, because deflating IV took more than the move gave.
etym: From «to straddle» — to stand with legs apart: the position sits on both sides of price.

short: The price at which an option is exercised, if it is exercised.
full: The strike is fixed in the contract and does not move, while the asset's market price wanders around it — and it is precisely the gap between the two that decides whether the option is worth anything at expiry. The set of strikes for one date forms the implied-volatility «smile»: equidistant strikes are usually priced differently, and that skew by itself tells you which move the market fears more.
etym: From «strike price» — the price at which the trade strikes when exercised.

short: A price level where demand has historically exceeded supply, halting a decline.
full: A support level is a horizontal zone where price has repeatedly stopped falling and turned back up. Buyers tend to become active near these zones. The more times price has tested a level without breaking it, the more significant that support is considered. Once broken, support often turns into resistance — the flip. Support levels are used to place stop-losses and to look for entries on retests.
etym: From "support" — the floor that holds price up.

short: The charge or credit for holding an FX position overnight.
full: The two currencies' rate differential accrues daily: one side of the trade pays you, the other costs you. The broker adds its own margin, so credits are usually smaller than theory and debits larger. Wednesdays often carry a triple swap, covering the weekend. For positions held beyond a week the swap stops being a detail and enters the arithmetic alongside the spread.
etym: From «swap» — the exchange of interest payments between two currencies.

short: An order that closes a position automatically once the profit target is reached.
full: A take-profit (TP) locks in profit at a predefined level and is used alongside a stop-loss. The ratio of TP to SL is the risk-to-reward (R:R). A common minimum is 1:2 — profit twice the risk — which leaves a system profitable at a 34% win rate. Closing part of the position at the first target and moving the stop to breakeven is a widespread way to manage the rest.
etym: From "take profit" — literally, take the profit.

short: The extra return demanded for lending long rather than short.
full: A long bond's yield is expected short rates plus the term premium — compensation for the uncertainty of the future. The premium cannot be observed directly, only modelled, which is exactly why it is argued over. Practically: when long yields rise without any change in rate expectations, it is usually the premium rising — the market is asking more for the same maturity.
etym: Literally the premium paid for «term», the time to maturity.

short: How much value an option loses per day from the passage of time alone.
full: Theta is negative for the buyer and positive for the seller: time works for whoever collected the premium. Decay accelerates into expiry, so short-dated options melt noticeably faster. Hence the rule beginners learn expensively: a bought option loses money even in a flat market, and profit needs not just the right direction but the right direction in time.
etym: The eighth Greek letter, chosen for the initial of «time» in the English tradition.

short: The time interval each candle on a chart covers (M30, H1, H4, D1, W1).
full: A timeframe is the period one candle represents. M1/M5/M15 suit scalping and intraday work. M30/H1 are intraday and swing. H4/D1 are medium-term. W1/MN are long-term. The multi-timeframe principle: read the trend on the higher timeframe, find the entry on the lower one. Levels drawn on a higher timeframe carry more weight than those on a lower one.
etym: The frame of time a single candle covers.

short: The gap between a country's exports and imports over a period.
full: A surplus means the country sells more than it buys; a deficit the reverse. For the currency what matters is not the sign itself but the change and how it is financed: a persistent deficit with capital inflows can run for decades, as in the US. Exports and imports are read separately: both falling together usually signals a slowdown rather than an improving balance.
etym: «Balance» as in the remainder after flows are netted against each other.

short: US Treasury debt — the world's reference for the risk-free rate.
full: Treasuries split by maturity: Bills under a year, Notes from two to ten years, Bonds out to thirty. The ten-year yield is the most quoted rate on the planet: the cost of money, US mortgages and equity valuations are all read off it. They are called risk-free in the credit sense — repayment is near-certain. Interest-rate and inflation risk remain in full.
etym: From the US Treasury, the department that issues them.

short: A sustained directional move: up (bullish), down (bearish) or sideways (range).
full: A trend is defined by its sequence of extremes: bullish means higher highs and higher lows, bearish means lower highs and lower lows. A range is horizontal, with no clear direction. Dow's axiom holds that a trend is in force until proven otherwise. Identifying the trend is the first step of any analysis, and trading with it reduces the odds of a bad trade.
etym: From "trend" — the prevailing direction of price.

short: A narrowing range: highs and lows converge.
full: Narrowing means falling volatility — accumulation before a move. The shape says nothing about direction, despite the popular «ascending» and «descending» readings. There is one useful and measurable property: the range on exit is usually wider than inside, so a squeeze is grounds for preparing a plan for both directions rather than predicting one.
etym: From the geometric shape formed by the converging boundary lines.

short: The total value of assets deposited in a DeFi protocol.
full: TVL is used as a size measure, but it has two flaws. First, it is denominated in dollars, so it rises and falls with token prices even when nothing is deposited or withdrawn. Second, the same asset pledged along a chain of protocols is counted several times. TVL therefore reads better as a trend than as a sum.
etym: Total Value Locked — funds locked inside contracts.

short: Execution in equal slices at equal intervals of time.
full: TWAP cuts a large order into pieces and releases them by the clock, ignoring volume. That is how it differs from VWAP, which adapts to market activity. The simplicity is both virtue and weakness: the algorithm is predictable, and its presence is detectable if you look, through regular identical trades. It is used where volume data are sparse or the market is uneven.
etym: Time Weighted Average Price.

short: The share of people seeking work within the labour force.
full: The series is treacherous because it falls for two opposite reasons: people found jobs — or stopped looking and dropped out of the count. It is therefore read alongside the participation rate. The Sahm rule, popular since 2022, uses exactly this series: a 0.5-point rise in the three-month average off the year's low has historically coincided with the onset of recession.
etym: In statistics the unemployed are not everyone without a job, only those actively seeking one.

short: The option price's sensitivity to a change in implied volatility.
full: Vega shows how much an option gains or loses when IV rises by one percentage point. It is larger for longer-dated and near-the-money options. Vega explains a common story: the event passes, price moves the right way, yet the bought option is cheaper — because uncertainty left with the event, IV collapsed, and vega took more than direction gave.
etym: The only «Greek» absent from the Greek alphabet: the name is borrowed from the star Vega.

short: The expected 30-day volatility of the S&P 500 — the market's "fear gauge".
full: The VIX (CBOE Volatility Index) is derived from S&P 500 option prices. Below 15 the market is calm. Between 20 and 30 there is moderate uncertainty. Above 30 signals high anxiety, often near a market bottom. It is inversely correlated with the S&P 500: when the index falls, the VIX rises. The VIX says nothing about direction, only about amplitude. Crypto has an equivalent in DVOL, the Deribit volatility index for BTC.
etym: Introduced by the CBOE in 1993 as a measure of expected market volatility.

short: A measure of how widely price swings over a period.
full: Volatility measures how far price strays from its average. High volatility means large candles, wide spreads and strong moves; low volatility means narrow candles and a quiet market. ATR (Average True Range) is a popular measure of historical volatility. Implied volatility (IV) is the volatility the market expects, priced into options. For equities the benchmark is the VIX, the "fear index". Volatility usually compresses ahead of a release and jumps after it.
etym: From the Latin volatilis — flying, fleeting.

short: The number of lots, contracts or coins traded over a period.
full: Volume is an important secondary indicator. A move on high volume carries more weight. A rally on thin volume is a potentially weak signal, and falling volume inside a trend warns of a possible reversal. A volume profile shows at which prices the most trading took place; the Point of Control — the price with the highest traded volume — often acts as support or resistance.
etym: From "volume" — the amount traded.

short: The distribution of volume across prices rather than across time.
full: An ordinary volume histogram answers «when it traded»; the profile answers «at what price». The level with the greatest volume is called the point of control: there the market agreed with the price longest, and returns to it are frequent. Low-volume zones are crossed quickly — which is why moves between dense levels look like jumps. The tool describes structure; it does not forecast.
etym: «Profile» as a side view: volume is unrolled along the vertical price axis, like a relief profile.

short: The average price over a period, weighted by traded volume.
full: VWAP serves two different purposes. For a large participant it is a benchmark of execution quality: buying below VWAP means doing better than the day's average. For a retail trader it is an intraday magnet that price frequently rejects from — precisely because algorithms reference it. Unlike a moving average, VWAP is computed from the session's open.
etym: Volume Weighted Average Price.

short: The share of profitable trades — the most commonly misread metric there is.
full: A high win rate is easy to achieve: take profit quickly and let losses run. Such a system looks superb until the first large trade eats everything accumulated. Win rate therefore means something only alongside the average ratio of win to loss. The breakeven threshold is simple arithmetic: stop divided by the sum of target and stop.
etym: From «win rate» — the frequency of winning outcomes.

short: The US benchmark crude, delivered at Cushing, Oklahoma.
full: WTI is lighter and cleaner than Brent but trades inland: delivery runs into Cushing storage, and how full that single hub is moves the price. Hence the well-known April 2020 episode — a negative price on the May contract: there was nowhere to store, yet the obligation to take delivery remained. The grade is the US market's reference and is quoted on CME.
etym: West Texas Intermediate — for its region of production and its mid-range density.

short: One issuer's yields across maturities, from a month to thirty years.
full: A normal curve slopes up: the longer you part with money, the more you ask. Its shape is a compressed summary of expectations — the short end follows the central bank's rate, the long end follows growth and inflation expectations. The curve therefore reads as the market's view of the future, and a view paid for with money rather than voiced in an interview.
etym: Literally the curve of yields: maturity along the axis, yield as the value.
